L7: # Verifying Account Ecosystems With Graph Transformations
L8: 
L9:   * Freya Murphy
L10:   * , 【5†Saša Radomirović】
L11: 
L12:   * 【6†School of Mathematical & Computer Sciences】
L13:   * 【7†Computer Science】
L14: 
L15: Research output: Chapter in Book/Report/Conference proceeding › Conference contribution
L16: 
L17: 13 Downloads (Pure)
L18: ## Abstract
L19: Account ecosystems comprise a set of resources, including online accounts, devices, and credentials, that jointly impact a user’s or organisation’s security. Prior work shows that users frequently overlook subtle dependencies within these ecosystems, leading to security breaches that are difficult to detect using analysis techniques focused on isolated components.We introduce resource access graphs (RAGs), a formal model for the automated analysis of dynamic account ecosystems.
L20: RAGs extend previous work on account access graphs (AAGs) with partially ordered labels for vertices and edges, enabling both general and resource-specific actions to be modelled. To capture the dynamic nature of account ecosystems, we define a transition system based on graph rewriting with RAGs as states in which both user actions and adversarial capabilities are modelled as graph transformation rules.
L21: Security properties are specified in computation tree logic (CTL) allowing analysis using existing graph-rewriting based model checkers, such as GROOVE.We demonstrate our approach on a simple Apple account ecosystem with the recent security feature Stolen Device Protection (SDP). Our analysis reveals limitations in SDP, affecting both the integrity and availability of a user’s Apple Account and we propose and verify an improvement to enhance account integrity.

L553@P21: 5.1 Management Considerations
L554@P21: Blockchain AC system management needs to coordinate with the business and resource
L555@P21: requirements of the system. For instance, a federated AC system may spread over multiple
L556@P21: organizations for cooperation and communication between participating organizations. Hence, AC
L557@P21: policies needs to be flexible and fine-grained. A blockchain AC system can transform the policy
L558@P21: evaluation process to executable smart contracts so that each organization can control its own
L559@P21: system while communicating with other federated organizations. Optionally, some federation
L560@P21: schemes may use the blockchain as a database for storing only the policies but not use the
L561@P21: blockchain for access enforcement, such that PDP and PEP functions are performed off-the-chain.

L563@P21: inherited [GBHC]. In addition, considerations should include governance frameworks for legal
L564@P21: processes, applicable smart contracts, and the responsibilities of participating AC nodes even
L565@P21: though the AC system is based on permissioned blockchains.

L549@P21: 5 Considerations
L550@P21: This section discusses considerations for the implementation of the blockchain AC system from
L551@P21: the perspectives of the management, security, privacy, performance, and standardization of AC
L552@P21: systems.
L553@P21: 5.1 Management Considerations
L554@P21: Blockchain AC system management needs to coordinate with the business and resource
L555@P21: requirements of the system. For instance, a federated AC system may spread over multiple
L556@P21: organizations for cooperation and communication between participating organizations. Hence, AC
L557@P21: policies needs to be flexible and fine-grained. A blockchain AC system can transform the policy
L558@P21: evaluation process to executable smart contracts so that each organization can control its own
L559@P21: system while communicating with other federated organizations. Optionally, some federation
L560@P21: schemes may use the blockchain as a database for storing only the policies but not use the
L561@P21: blockchain for access enforcement, such that PDP and PEP functions are performed off-the-chain.
L562@P21: However, the main problems of the traditional mechanism, like single point of failure, will be
L563@P21: inherited [GBHC]. In addition, considerations should include governance frameworks for legal
L564@P21: processes, applicable smart contracts, and the responsibilities of participating AC nodes even
L565@P21: though the AC system is based on permissioned blockchains.
L566@P21: Another challenge of managing blockchain AC systems is to develop a trust management and
L567@P21: evaluation framework for the decentralization of constrained resource systems, such as an IoT
L568@P21: network, where each AC node embedded in a device has limited battery power, memory capacity,
L569@P21: and processing speed, and it is often impossible to store extensive interaction history or employ
L570@P21: heavy-weight security functions (e.g., microservice of mesh service for SecDevOps
L571@P21: implementation).
L572@P21: General AC management requirements, such as allowing runtime policy rule changes and policy
L573@P21: administration delegation, may further complicate the design of the blockchain AC system,
L574@P21: especially the consensus mechanisms and smart contract functions [IR7874].
L575@P21: 5.2 Security Considerations
L576@P21: Any vulnerability of a blockchain AC system on the level of the entire system or an underlying
L577@P21: function of a smart contract can be hacked (e.g., reentrancy vulnerability) or misused. For instance,
L578@P21: the publicly available smart contract’s byte code might generate erroneous system state data that
L579@P21: will be securely logged on the blockchain. The only way to fix errors is to delete, correct, and
L580@P21: redeploy the entire smart contract. Thus, it is necessary for smart contracts to be correctly deployed
L581@P21: (i.e., they work as intended by the developer and cannot be exploited by attackers).
L582@P21: Optimizing smart contract codes can effectively reduce potential vulnerabilities and ensure the
L583@P21: efficient execution of contracts. For instance, running smart contracts in parallel can speed up
L584@P21: contract execution but requires the consideration of how to execute contracts that depend on each
